Stated Claim / Post Context:
Meta is dragging the UK’s online safety regime through the courts

Legal challenges brought by Meta threaten the building blocks of how the U.K.’s Online Safety Act is enforced.

Actual Article Body:
Legal challenges brought by Meta threaten the building blocks of how the U.K.’s Online Safety Act is enforced.

AI generated Text-to-speech

LONDON — This week, social media giants Meta, TikTok and X took the U.K.’s media regulator to court over its enforcement of the country’s flagship Online Safety Act.

Meta’s lawyers will be seeing Ofcom in court again very soon.

The High Court is scheduled to hear another challenge to the regulator from Meta next week, concerning how it calculates fees payable by certain regulated online services as well as penalties for breaches.

This year, the tech giant has launched three separate challenges against Ofcom related to online safety regulation.

Meta isn’t alone. Other companies have lodged similar challenges — but it is the most prolific in the wave of Big Tech litigation Ofcom currently faces.

The challenges could undermine the building blocks of the U.K.’s online safety regime and force the regulator to change course at the very moment it is preparing to take on responsibility for enforcing the upcoming under-16s social media ban.

A Meta spokesperson said legal challenges are a “normal feature of any new regulatory regime being bedded in and ensures questions of process, scope and implementation get settled so the law is applied proportionately, accurately and consistently.”

“We’re committed to working constructively with Ofcom as it enforces the Online Safety Act. Like many others in the industry, including TikTok, Roblox, X, and Quora, we are challenging specific aspects of implementation. These are not challenges to the law itself, but how Ofcom has interpreted it,” they said.

Aspects of the regime were “always going to be tested in the courts,” Lorna Woods, adviser at the Online Safety Network said. “However, the impact of litigation on the regulator and the regulatory regime goes beyond the substance of the particular claim. It has the effect of tying up regulatory attention, training public resources and in general pushing the regulator to adopt a more cautious stance generally.”

Here are the parts of the U.K.’s online safety regime Meta is challenging — and why they matter.

Meta says Ofcom’s methodology for calculating fees and potential penalties under the OSA should be based on a company’s U.K. revenue, rather than its global revenue.

Breaches of the OSA can attract fines of up to 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue or £18 million, whichever is greater. Given Meta reported roughly $200 billion in global revenue last year, any theoretical penalty would almost certainly be more than £18 million.

Certain regulated services also have to pay Ofcom annual fees under the OSA totalling around 0.02% to 0.03% of qualifying worldwide revenue, per Ofcom estimates. Meta also wants these calculated — i.e. reduced — based on U.K. rather than global revenue.

If the court rules in Meta’s favor, Ofcom will need to redesign its entire approach to fees and penalties. Digital rights nonprofit 5Rights, which has been granted permission to intervene in support of Ofcom, will argue next week that parliament intended the Online Safety Act to provide for substantial fines pegged to global revenue.

“The Online Safety Act cannot be a paper tiger. Parliament intended it to provide a strong deterrent. Effective enforcement is what turns regulation into meaningful change. Without it, the promise of safer technology for children will remain unfulfilled,” 5Rights Executive Director Leanda Barrington Leach said.

Meta, along with TikTok and X, is also challenging Ofcom’s information gathering powers. The three social media companies put their arguments to the court this week.

In a skeleton argument seen by POLITICO, Meta’s lawyers argued that three notices issued by Ofcom in February requesting content moderation metrics constituted a “wish list” with no legal basis.

Ofcom countered that it needs this information to assess how well safety measures are working and redesign interventions if needed.

The OSA requires Ofcom to publish and maintain a register of “categorized” online services which are subject to extra duties. The most onerous of these are reserved for so-called “Category 1” services, and include giving users greater choice and control over the content they see.

Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp were all designated Category 1 by Ofcom, but Meta appealed against Instagram and WhatsApp’s inclusion last month.

Already Meta’s appeal threatens to gum up the regime: under the OSA, additional duties — like tackling fraudulent advertising — get suspended until appeals are resolved.

These duties are some of the most significant in the OSA and are designed to address many of the online harms adult users complain about that aren’t covered elsewhere in the legislation.

Ofcom officials told peers last month that they envisage the duties being fully in force by the middle of next year — already delayed a year partly thanks to a judicial review brought by the non-profit Wikimedia Foundation — but that timeline could slip because of Meta’s appeal.

Video game company Roblox also indicated an intention to appeal its Category 1 status.

An Ofcom spokesperson said that the OSA means “Parliament has charged us with the job of regulating an industry that has been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years.”

“Effective regulation relies on our ability to gather information, levy appropriate fees, issue fines and apply the law as intended. While legal challenges are an important part of any regulatory regime, we will defend them robustly as part of our mission of making life safer online for people in the U.K.,” they added.

Through these various legal challenges Meta has opted to take its differences of opinion with the regulator public. This week, Ofcom did the same when it launched an investigation into Meta over whether the company had properly risk-assessed new feature called “Instagram Instants” before launch.

The move was welcomed by online safety campaigners, who’ve long urged Ofcom to show more muscle.

A Meta spokesperson said the company “takes its regulatory obligations under the Online Safety Act seriously,” adding: “We conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom about this feature on a number of occasions before launching it.”

Meta's spokesperson said the company will “of course co-operate with Ofcom during this investigation.”

Ofcom is worried Pornhub over-relied on Apple’s age checks to keep kids off its platform.

The U.K. can learn from Australia and France’s attempts to kick kids off social media.

Reform UK said GDPR has “strangled small businesses and tech firms.”

The science behind kicking kids off social media is murky at best, and experts say it could backfire.
